messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
Anant is eighty years old, a widower who served forty years with the Coast Guard, and for most of his life, his pride was anchored to the uniform he wore. That changed six months ago on a squally Tuesday in October. He was volunteering, skippering a small tour boat for a local conservation society off the coast of Maine. The fog had rolled in thick and fast, a sudden grey wall that swallowed the horizon. He was navigating by instruments, confident in his decades of experience, when the impact came—a sickening crunch of fibreglass and a high, sharp scream. He had struck a small pleasure craft, nearly invisible in the haze. The young woman at its helm was thrown against the console, her leg shattered. The memory of her pale, shocked face as the paramedics worked, the wail of the sirens echoing across the water, is the last clear thing he remembers from that day.

In the weeks that followed, the event refused to settle into a coherent story in his mind. When Anant tried to deliberately recall the sequence of events, he found only a frustrating void. Yet, the memory would ambush him in other ways, not as a narrative but as a sensory assault. The smell of salt and diesel, the specific shade of grey of the fog, the jarring thud that seemed to reverberate up through the soles of his feet—these fragments would erupt without warning, feeling utterly and terrifyingly real. This terrifying reliving of disconnected moments only heightened his sense of constant, unpredictable danger. He began to feel that he had to be on guard at all times, because an attack could come from anywhere, even from within his own mind. His home, once a sanctuary, became a place of potential ambushes. He started choosing his chair in the living room based on its view of the door and window, a habit he couldn't explain but couldn't break.

The triggers are everywhere. A walk in the state park behind his house, once his greatest pleasure, is now a minefield; the damp, earthy smell and the sound of wind in the pines are too similar to the coastal headlands of that day. This immersion in nature instantly brings back shards of the memory—the splintered wood, the cry—and with them, a surge of adrenaline that tells him he is unsafe. He finds himself scanning the trees, his heart pounding, before retreating back to his car. Even the sound of a distant ambulance siren sends a jolt of terror through him, activating a profound sense of threat that makes him feel as though disaster is imminent. In these moments of heightened alert, the memories become more accessible, more vivid, as if his brain is trying to find the source of the danger in the past. This constant sense of being on guard has, over time, cemented a devastating conclusion in his mind: the world is a dangerous place, and he is no longer competent to navigate it.

This belief has become the lens through which he sees everything. He has come to believe the accident wasn't just a mistake born of fog and bad luck, but a reflection of a fundamental flaw in his character. "A good man, a careful man, wouldn't have let that happen," he repeats to himself. This painful appraisal—that there is something wrong with him as a person—is a constant, heavy presence. It makes any conversation about the future, especially his grandchildren's, feel like a personal indictment, a reminder of the future he nearly stole from that young woman. To escape the acute shame of these thoughts, Anant has developed a series of frantic mental maneuvers. He tries to forcefully push the images out of his head, or he tells himself the event didn't really happen, that it was just a terrible dream. Sometimes he forces himself to think only of positive things, like his late wife’s smile, in a desperate attempt to paper over the horror.

But these strategies are failing. Trying to suppress the memories only seems to make them stronger, and the effort leaves him exhausted and more attuned to his triggers. The constant feeling of threat forces him to avoid any unfamiliar places, shrinking his world to his house and the corner store. The magical thinking, his attempt to deny reality, only deepens his conviction that he is defective, because a sane person, he reasons, wouldn't have to lie to himself to get through the day. The entire system now feeds itself. A trigger, like a siren, creates a sense of threat, which dredges up a memory fragment. The memory reinforces his negative belief that he is a dangerous person, which is so painful he must use a strategy like thought suppression to cope. But the suppression leaves the memory unprocessed and sharp, ready to be activated by the next trigger, which his hypervigilant state is now actively scanning for. His life has become a tightening loop of fear and self-blame. He finally sought help last week after his eldest grandson, a high school senior, announced he was thinking of enlisting in the Coast Guard. Anant couldn't conjure a single positive word. He just stared, his mind filled with the sound of splintering fibreglass, and had to leave the room. He is terrified that this thing inside him will not only consume his past, but also destroy his connection to his family's future.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not state that triggers directly cause negative beliefs about himself or the world.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not state that his negative beliefs cause him to be more aware of or search for triggers.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette does not state that the trauma memory directly causes him to use maladaptive coping strategies.
  e.g. "She had learned that if she kept the television on loud enough, the thoughts couldn't get a foothold — silence was the enemy."
  e.g. "After the memory surfaced during sex, she began finding quiet reasons to avoid intimacy altogether, telling herself she was simply tired or stressed."
  e.g. "To stop the images coming at night, she started staying up later and later, until exhaustion was the only reliable way to fall asleep."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not state that experiencing the trauma memory makes him more sensitive or attentive to triggers.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: The vignette does not state that using maladaptive strategies increases his overall sense of threat.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Even the sound of a distant ambulance siren sends a jolt of terror through him, activating a profound sense of threat that makes him feel as though disaster is imminent.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
That piercing wail on the wind is not just a warning of external danger; it has become a personal judgment, confirming his belief that he is now fundamentally unsafe to be around.
<<<END>>>
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
This belief has become the lens through which he sees everything.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
His conviction that he is no longer competent means that things he once would have registered and dismissed—the low rumble of a boat engine, a patch of morning fog—now snag his attention, standing out as potential signs of another failure.
<<<END>>>
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
This painful appraisal—that there is something wrong with him as a person—is a constant, heavy presence.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Whenever the memory of the woman's pale, shocked face comes to mind, he immediately tries to forcefully push the image away or tells himself the event wasn't real, desperate to stop the sensory replay before it can take hold.
<<<END>>>
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
The smell of salt and diesel, the specific shade of grey of the fog, the jarring thud that seemed to reverberate up through the soles of his feet—these fragments would erupt without warning, feeling utterly and terrifyingly real.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
After one of these sensory flashbacks, he is left hyper-alert, and the world seems full of echoes of the trauma; the sound of wind in the pines or the damp smell of his basement becomes a potential harbinger of the memory's return.
<<<END>>>
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
The constant feeling of threat forces him to avoid any unfamiliar places, shrinking his world to his house and the corner store.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
This avoidance has become a trap; by never testing his fear, he has no way to learn that the world is not as dangerous as his body insists it is, and so the feeling of threat remains perpetually high.
<<<END>>>
